Start reading here

Start with the Association’s own 2000 testimony, which situates Angoon in a Tlingit community’s relationships with Admiralty Island and coastal waters. Then read the historical and educational sources alongside it. This is a bounded guide to a named local tribal government and community, with substantial history still to develop. Read source annotations for selected pages, dates, perspective and access limits. This is not a complete history or community endorsement.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A community history and a dated organization

The Association’s charter was ratified in November 1939 and printed in 1940. Its stated purpose included improving community members’ economic circumstances. That documentary date belongs to the Association’s organizational history; it does not date the beginnings of the Tlingit community. A 2024 Sealaska Heritage Institute notice provides another historical entry point, connecting a planned Navy apology to the 1882 bombardment and the loss of shelter and provisions that followed.

Read the sources [2] U.S. Government Printing Office; University of Oklahoma Law Library transcription [4] Sealaska Heritage Institute

02

Speaking for coastal relationships

At an EPA hearing in September 2000, Tim June read a letter from the Association’s environmental department. It described Angoon as a Tlingit community connected to Admiralty Island and surrounding food resources. The letter raised concerns about cruise ships’ effects on water, fish and wildlife. This is a dated example of the Association advocating for coastal protection; the testimony is not presented as current environmental data.

Read the sources [1] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, hearing transcript

03

Tlingit learning in the local school

Angoon School’s account of its May 2025 Culture Camp Week names Tlingit language teacher Pauline Johnson as its organizer. Students worked with storytelling, books, weaving, sewing, art and digital storytelling. The account makes cultural education visible as work undertaken by teachers, students and community members. It describes a particular school event and does not establish participation or language ability for all Association citizens.

Read the sources [3] Chatham School District / Angoon School

Tribal testimony in government transcriptU.S. Environmental Protection Agency, hearing transcriptSource 1

Angoon Community Association testimony in EPA Public Meeting #12227, September 8, 2000 ↗

Publication: 2000-09-08

A direct community statement about the relationship between surrounding waters, food resources and responsibility for environmental protection. Read this as testimony submitted in 2000, not as present environmental monitoring results.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Printed pages 143–145 (PDF pages 142–144), opening and selected continuation of the Association letter: speaker attribution, Admiralty Island/Tlingit community setting and cruise-ship environmental concerns. Not the full hearing or a complete review of the letter.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Web reader timed out on the PDF. The public EPA snapshot PDF was downloaded successfully once with ordinary urllib access. Selected text extracted with pypdf; all three selected page renders viewed. No current legal or pollution conclusions adopted.

https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/sites/static/files/2015-11/documents/juneau_alaska_hearing_transcript.pdf

Corporate Charter of the Angoon Community Association, Alaska ↗

Publication: 1940; ratified 1939-11-15

A dated primary record of the Association’s charter and economic purposes. It helps distinguish the organization’s twentieth-century documentary history from the much longer history of the community.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Title and imprint; preamble; purpose and management clauses; certification of November 15, 1939 ratification. Remaining powers clauses were visible but are not interpreted as current law.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Public body readable through the web reader; only the stated selected body was reviewed.

https://thorpe.law.ou.edu/IRA/angoonchrtr.html

Watch live: Military to apologize to Angoon for bombardment ↗

Publication: 2024-10-21

A short Native institutional notice linking the planned 2024 Navy apology to the 1882 attack and its aftermath. It is a starting point for community-directed historical reading, not a full account of the event or its acceptance.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Entire short notice including date, scheduled October 26 event, and paragraph on destruction of shelter and provisions in 1882. Linked video/program not inspected.
